lesson.title: The Power That Isn't Spent: Reactive Power
lesson.summary: Reactive power measures the energy that sloshes back and forth between a source and an inductor or capacitor every cycle without ever being consumed.
lesson.body:
Average power captures only part of the story of how hard a source works to drive an AC load. A circuit containing inductance or capacitance also exchanges energy with the source every cycle, energy stored in a magnetic or electric field for a quarter cycle and then returned in full, never consumed. This back-and-forth exchange still requires current to flow and still requires the source and wiring to be sized for it, even though, averaged over a cycle, it delivers zero net energy; the quantity that measures the size of this exchange is reactive power, Q.

Reactive power is defined as Q = Vrms Irms sin θ, where θ is the same impedance angle used in the average power formula, measured in volt-amperes reactive, or VAR, rather than watts, specifically to keep it visually distinct from real, dissipated power. The sin θ factor mirrors the cos θ factor in average power: at θ = 0°, pure resistance, sin θ = 0 and there is no reactive power at all; at θ = ±90°, pure reactance, sin θ = ±1 and every bit of apparent power is reactive, none of it real.

For the series RL circuit, Vrms = 120 V, Irms = 2.4 A, and θ = 53.13°. Reactive power is Q = 120 × 2.4 × sin(53.13°) = 288 × 0.8000 = 230.4 VAR. This positive value reflects the inductive nature of the load, current lagging voltage, by convention. Physically, this 230.4 VAR represents energy sloshing into the inductor's magnetic field and back out again, twice per cycle, without ever leaving the circuit as heat, light, or motion; only the 172.8 W of average power computed in the previous section actually leaves the source for good.

Reactive power connects directly back to reactance: it exists only because XL, or XC, is nonzero, and its magnitude grows with both the current magnitude and the size of that reactance. Utilities and equipment designers care about Q because the current producing it is real current, it heats wires and loads transformers exactly like the current that produces average power, even though it delivers no useful energy to the load. Reactive power and average power are not simply added together as ordinary numbers, since they represent energy flows at right angles to each other in a phasor sense; combining them correctly is the job of apparent power, taken up next.

Just as average power can be checked with P = Irms² R, reactive power has an analogous check using reactance alone: Q = Irms² X. For the series RL circuit, Irms = 2.4 A and X = XL = 40 Ω, so Q = (2.4)² × 40 = 5.76 × 40 = 230.4 VAR, matching the Vrms Irms sin θ calculation exactly. This parallel structure, P tied to R, Q tied to X, both scaled by Irms², is a direct consequence of impedance's rectangular form Z = R + jX: real power flows through the real part, reactive power through the imaginary part of that same complex number, with nothing lost or double-counted between the two.
